patient.name: Patricia Mensah
patient.setting: GP surgery, practice nurse leg ulcer clinic
patient.complaint: Weeping sore above the right inner ankle for 3 months
background: Varicose veins in both legs for 20 years
Right leg DVT 9 years ago after a hip replacement
BMI 34; retired school cook in Lewisham, on her feet all day for decades
No diabetes; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a shallow, mildly painful ulcer above the medial malleolus, brown hardened skin and palpable pulses. The distractors are arterial, neuropathic and pyoderma gangrenosum.

points: Patricia, 71, has a **weeping sore** above her right inner ankle.
It has been there **3 months** and keeps soaking her socks.
It only **aches mildly**; worse after a long day standing.
Her legs feel heavy and she gets **night cramps**.

steps.lead: Patricia's leaky leg veins keep her ankle under **venous hypertension**; the oedematous skin starves and breaks down.
She ticks three boxes for venous stasis: **varicose veins**, a **previous DVT** and obesity.

points: 4 cm **shallow** ulcer just above the **medial malleolus**.
Irregular edges, granulating base, lots of exudate.
Surrounding skin **brown, hard and eczematous**; pitting ankle oedema.
Foot warm; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses **palpable**.

steps.lead: Every feature fits: **gaiter region**, shallow and oozing, only mildly painful, brown skin and eczema around it.

steps.q: Which feature of Patricia's ulcer most favours a venous over an arterial cause?
o: Shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus
steps.r: Venous ulcers are **shallow, irregular and in the gaiter area**. Arterial ulcers are punched-out, painful and on toes or pressure points.

steps.lead: Patricia's right leg narrows just above the ankle and is swollen above it: the **inverted champagne bottle**.
Left alone, Patricia's ulcer may never heal and is a doorway for **cellulitis**.
If Patricia's pain suddenly worsened, the skin went black or she became unwell, you would think **arterial** or severe infection, not simple venous disease.

steps.text: A **painful, punched-out toe ulcer** with a cold foot is arterial, even in a patient with varicose veins. Site and pain decide, not the background.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (ABPI before compression) or a question on what confirms venous insufficiency (duplex ultrasound showing reflux).

steps.lead: Patricia's pulses are palpable, but the nurse still measures **ABPI** before any bandage goes on.

steps.title: Doppler pressures (mmHg)
steps.text: ABPI = highest ankle systolic divided by highest brachial systolic.

visual.title: Patricia's right ABPI
visual.label: Patricia 0.94
visual.caption: Above 0.8: her arterial supply is intact, so compression is safe.

steps.q: Patricia's ABPI is 0.94. What does this mean?
steps.r: An ABPI **above 0.8** confirms the arteries are fine, so the ulcer is not arterial and compression can start.

steps.lead: Patricia's diagnosis is clinical plus ABPI; a **duplex ultrasound** then shows the reflux in her veins.

steps.title: Working up a leg ulcer
nodes: Look: site, edge, base, surrounding skin
steps.caption: ABPI always comes before compression.

steps.text: A **high ABPI (>1.3)** is not reassuring. In diabetes or renal disease the calf arteries are calcified and will not compress, so the reading is falsely high.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where the ABPI decides: four-layer compression if 0.8–1.3, vascular referral if >1.3, and flucloxacillin if the ulcer is infected.

steps.title: Venous ulcer pathway
nodes: Healed → Class II stockings for life
Definitive: endovenous ablation of the refluxing vein
steps.caption: Infection and a high ABPI are the two side branches.

visual.title: ABPI decides the treatment
visual.label: Patricia 0.94
visual.caption: Patricia sits in the green band: full compression.

steps.lead: With arterial disease excluded, Patricia starts **four-layer compression bandaging**, changed weekly by the nurse.

steps.q: Patricia's ABPI is 0.94 and the ulcer is not infected. What is first-line treatment?
steps.r: **Four-layer bandaging** heals an active ulcer. Stockings are for after healing; ablation treats the underlying vein later.

points: Week 5: new **spreading redness** around the ulcer.
Leg warmer and more painful; more pus-like exudate.
Feels mildly feverish but otherwise well.

steps.lead: Patricia's ulcer has **cellulitis**. She has no penicillin allergy, so she gets **flucloxacillin**.

visual.title: Patricia's ulcer under compression
visual.caption: Steady healing with compression, a pause for infection, then closure by week 16.

steps.lead: Healed, Patricia moves to **Class II stockings** and is referred for **endovenous ablation** of her refluxing vein.
Had Patricia been diabetic with an ABPI of 1.4, stockings would be avoided and she would go to **vascular surgery**.

steps.text: Bandages heal the ulcer; **stockings** stop it coming back; **ablation** fixes the vein. Do not offer stockings to an open ulcer.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the ulcer sits at the medial malleolus, what causes the brown skin (haemosiderin) and why compression is dangerous with a low ABPI.

steps.lead: Patricia's DVT damaged her valves. Blood now falls back down, and pressure peaks over the **medial malleolus**.

steps.title: From leaky valve to ulcer
nodes: Poor oxygen and nutrient delivery to skin

visual.title: Ankle vein pressure while walking
visual.caption: Normally the calf pump empties the veins on walking. With leaky valves the pressure stays high.

steps.lead: The brown ring around Patricia's ulcer is **haemosiderin** from red cells that leaked out and broke down.

steps.q: What causes the brown pigmentation around Patricia's ulcer?
steps.r: Red cells leak out of high-pressure capillaries, break down and leave **haemosiderin** in the dermis.

steps.lead: Years of inflammation scarred Patricia's ankle fat (**lipodermatosclerosis**) into a tight band below a still-swollen calf.
Compression squeezes Patricia's veins and pushes oedema back, but on a leg with poor arteries it would cut off what little flow is left.

steps.text: Compression on a leg with significant arterial disease can cause **critical ischaemia**. That is why ABPI is measured every time.

mcq.q: What is the most common type of leg ulcer?
mcq.r: **Venous ulcers** are the most common leg ulcers.

mcq.q: Where is a venous ulcer classically found?
mcq.r: The **gaiter region**, classically over the medial malleolus.

mcq.q: Which leg shape is the signature of chronic venous disease?
mcq.r: Lipodermatosclerosis narrows the ankle below a swollen calf: the **inverted champagne bottle**.

mcq.q: Which complication is a venous ulcer especially prone to?
mcq.r: Venous ulcers are prone to secondary **cellulitis**.

mcq.q: What must be measured before applying compression bandages?
mcq.r: **ABPI** excludes significant arterial disease before compression.

mcq.q: What does duplex ultrasound show in venous insufficiency?
mcq.r: Duplex shows **retrograde venous flow** (reflux) through incompetent valves.

mcq.q: What is the first-line treatment for a venous ulcer with ABPI 0.8–1.3?
mcq.r: **Four-layer compression bandaging** once arterial disease is excluded.

mcq.q: Which antibiotic is first-line for an infected venous ulcer?
mcq.r: **Flucloxacillin**; clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic, co-amoxiclav if severe.

mcq.q: What ABPI should stop compression and prompt vascular referral?
mcq.r: ABPI **>1.3** means calcified, non-compressible vessels: refer to vascular surgery.

mcq.q: What causes the brown skin around a venous ulcer?

technique.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 4 month history of an ulcer on her left lower leg. She had a left leg DVT 12 years ago. The ulcer is shallow, 5 cm across and just above the medial malleolus, with an irregular edge and a moist granulating base. It is only mildly painful. The surrounding skin is brown and indurated. Foot pulses are palpable.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A leg ulcer diagnosis: decide by **site, edge, pain and the skin around it**.
Previous DVT is a risk factor; gaiter site, shallow, irregular, mild pain, haemosiderin and lipodermatosclerosis; pulses rule out arterial.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic venous insufficiency causing ulceration: **venous ulcer**.

elim: Arterial ulcers are punched-out, painful, on toes or pressure points, with weak pulses.
Neuropathic ulcers are painless and on the sole or metatarsal heads in diabetes.
Pressure ulcers sit over bony points such as the heel or sacrum in immobile patients.
Pyoderma gangrenosum is very painful with a purple undermined edge, often with IBD.

steps.x: **E. Venous ulcer.** Rule: shallow + medial malleolus + brown skin + pulses present = venous.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a chronic ulcer above his right medial malleolus with surrounding haemosiderin staining and venous eczema. His ABPI is 0.97. He has prominent varicose veins along the medial thigh and calf. The vascular team want to confirm the underlying venous insufficiency before planning ablation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks what **confirms the venous insufficiency**, not what to check before compression.
ABPI is already done and normal; the question is about the veins themselves.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Duplex ultrasound** shows retrograde flow through incompetent valves.

elim: ABPI is already done; it assesses arteries, not venous reflux.
CT angiography images arteries and is for arterial disease.
X-ray does not show venous flow; it is for osteomyelitis or foreign bodies.
A swab is only for suspected infection and does not confirm venous disease.

steps.x: **C. Duplex ultrasound.** ABPI before compression; duplex to confirm venous reflux.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has a shallow ulcer above his left medial malleolus with surrounding brown, hardened skin. His foot pulses are difficult to feel. His ABPI is 1.45 on the left. The ulcer is not infected.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Management of a venous-looking ulcer: the **ABPI** decides whether compression is safe.
Diabetes and CKD calcify arteries. ABPI >1.3 is falsely high, so arterial disease cannot be excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Avoid compression and **refer to vascular surgery**.

elim: Stockings must be avoided with ABPI >1.3, and are for healed ulcers anyway.
Four-layer bandaging is only safe with ABPI roughly 0.8–1.3.
Antibiotics are for an infected ulcer; this one is not.
Steroid cream may help venous eczema but does not address the unsafe ABPI.

steps.x: **D. Refer to vascular surgery.** ABPI >1.3 = calcified vessels: no compression.

technique.stem: A 62 year old woman has long-standing varicose veins and a chronic shallow ulcer over her medial malleolus. Duplex ultrasound shows reflux through incompetent valves in the great saphenous vein. Her ABPI is 1.0.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her ulcer?

steps.x: It asks for the **mechanism**, so link the finding to the physiology.
Valve incompetence means blood falls back and the venous pressure stays high. Normal ABPI excludes arterial disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sustained venous hypertension** causes oedema, poor skin perfusion and breakdown.

elim: ABPI 1.0 means normal arterial supply.
Vasculitic ulcers are painful, multiple and come with systemic features.
Loss of sensation causes neuropathic ulcers on the sole.
Nothing suggests malignancy, and lymphoedema does not usually ulcerate this way.

steps.x: **E. Sustained venous hypertension.** Valves fail, pressure stays high, skin starves.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has a 5 month history of a weeping ulcer on her right lower leg. She has had varicose veins for many years and is obese. The ulcer lies above the medial malleolus, is shallow with irregular edges and is only mildly painful. The surrounding skin is brown with eczema. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. Foot pulses are present.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A shallow, mildly painful, exudative ulcer above the medial malleolus with brown skin and palpable pulses is a venous ulcer. Arterial ulcers are punched-out and painful with poor pulses.

steps.x: Leg ulcer diagnosis: site, edge, pain, surrounding skin, pulses.
Venous risk factors, gaiter site, venous look and venous skin changes, arteries intact.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Venous ulcer** from chronic venous insufficiency.

elim: Arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out and on the toes, with weak pulses.
Neuropathic ulcers are painless and on the sole in diabetes.
Pressure ulcers are over bony points in immobile patients.
Pyoderma is exquisitely painful with a violaceous undermined edge.

steps.x: **B. Chronic venous ulcer.** The gaiter area plus brown skin gives it away.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man has a shallow, exudative ulcer above his left medial malleolus that has been present for 6 months. He had a left femoral DVT 8 years ago. The ulcer aches after standing at work. His foot pulses are easily palpable.
practice.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination of the left leg?
practice.e: Chronic venous hypertension causes lipodermatosclerosis (hard, brown, fibrosed skin) around the ankle. Shiny hairless skin and a cold foot are arterial signs.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: decide the diagnosis, then pick its sign.
Classic venous ulcer after a DVT, with normal arteries.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous disease: expect **lipodermatosclerosis**, haemosiderin, eczema, oedema.

elim: Pulses are easily palpable; loss of pulses is arterial.
A cold, pale foot means arterial insufficiency.
Punched-out toe ulcers are arterial.
Shiny hairless skin is chronic arterial ischaemia.

steps.x: **C. Lipodermatosclerosis.** Venous skin is brown, hard and eczematous, not cold and shiny.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man who works as a security guard has a chronic shallow ulcer over his right medial malleolus. He had a right leg DVT after a fracture 10 years ago. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. His ABPI is 1.05 and the surrounding skin is pigmented.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his ulcer?
practice.e: A previous DVT damages venous valves; incompetence causes venous hypertension and ulceration at the medial malleolus. A normal ABPI excludes arterial disease.

steps.x: It asks the **cause**, so link the history to the pathology.

clues: DVT after a fracture 10 years ago
steps.x: Long standing plus post-DVT valve damage; normal ABPI; haemosiderin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-thrombotic **valvular incompetence** causing venous hypertension.

elim: ABPI 1.05 is normal; arterial disease is excluded.
No diabetes, and neuropathic ulcers are on the sole.
Footwear pressure causes ulcers on the toes or heel, not the gaiter area.
Malignant change (Marjolin) is rare and would need a raised, rolled or growing edge.

steps.x: **E. Venous valvular incompetence.** Previous DVT is a key venous ulcer risk factor.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman has had a venous ulcer above her left medial malleolus for a year. Over 2 days, the skin around it has become red, hot and swollen, with the redness spreading up the shin. She feels shivery. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Pain is in proportion to the findings and there is no crepitus.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Spreading warm erythema with fever and raised inflammatory markers around a venous ulcer is secondary cellulitis. Necrotising fasciitis causes pain out of proportion, crepitus and rapid deterioration.

steps.x: A diagnosis of a **complication** of a known venous ulcer.
Acute spreading infection with fever; no features of necrotising infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Secondary **cellulitis**, the classic venous ulcer complication.

elim: DVT causes calf swelling and pain, not spreading erythema from an ulcer with fever and high WCC.
Lipodermatosclerosis is chronic, hard and brown, not acutely hot.
Necrotising fasciitis needs pain out of proportion, crepitus or rapid systemic collapse.
Venous eczema is itchy and scaly without fever.

steps.x: **A. Cellulitis.** Venous ulcers are prone to secondary cellulitis.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has chronic venous insufficiency with recurrent ulcers above both medial malleoli. Over many years his lower legs have changed shape. The skin just above each ankle is hard, brown and bound down, while the calves above remain swollen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely appearance of his lower legs?
practice.e: Lipodermatosclerosis narrows the ankle while the calf above stays oedematous, giving the inverted champagne bottle leg of chronic venous disease.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question about the shape of the leg.
Fibrosed narrow ankle below a swollen calf.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **inverted champagne bottle** leg.

elim: Calf hypertrophy is seen in muscular dystrophies, not venous disease.
Gangrene is arterial.
Pale, shiny, hairless shins are chronic arterial ischaemia.
Whole-leg swelling suggests lymphoedema or an iliofemoral DVT, without ankle tapering.

steps.x: **C. Inverted champagne bottle.** Signature of chronic venous disease.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman with varicose veins and a previous DVT has heavy, aching legs and night cramps after long periods of standing. She has pitting ankle oedema and brown staining of the skin around both ankles. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg. Foot pulses are palpable. She is at risk of developing a venous ulcer.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site for a venous ulcer to develop?
practice.e: Venous ulcers form in the gaiter region, classically over the medial malleolus, where venous pressure is highest. Toes and heel are arterial or pressure sites.

steps.x: A 'where' question: recall the classic site.
Chronic venous insufficiency with skin changes and normal arteries.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **medial malleolus** in the gaiter area.

elim: The dorsum of the foot is not a typical venous site.
Heel ulcers are pressure or arterial.
The lateral malleolus is more typical of arterial or pressure ulcers.
Toe-tip ulcers are arterial.

steps.x: **D. Medial malleolus.** Highest venous pressure, worst skin damage.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has a shallow ulcer above her right medial malleolus with surrounding haemosiderin staining and pitting oedema. She has varicose veins. The practice nurse plans to start compression bandaging. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: ABPI must be measured before any compression to exclude significant arterial disease. A swab is only needed if the ulcer looks infected.

steps.x: The **initial** investigation, and the plan is compression.
Classic venous ulcer about to be compressed: arteries must be checked first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ABPI** before compression.

elim: CT angiography is for proven arterial disease needing intervention.
X-ray is for suspected osteomyelitis.
Venography is invasive and replaced by duplex ultrasound.
The ulcer shows no signs of infection, so a swab adds nothing.

steps.x: **A. ABPI.** No ABPI, no compression.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man has a healed venous ulcer and visible varicose veins along his medial calf. His ABPI is 1.02. He is referred to the vascular clinic to plan endovenous ablation, and a duplex ultrasound of the leg veins is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on duplex ultrasound?
o: Arterial stenosis at the adductor canal
practice.e: Duplex ultrasound confirms venous insufficiency by showing retrograde venous flow (reflux) through incompetent valves. Monophasic waveforms and stenoses are arterial findings.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' on the confirmatory test.
Venous disease with normal arteries; ablation targets a refluxing vein.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Retrograde venous flow** (reflux).

elim: Arterial stenosis would lower the ABPI; it is 1.02.
Monophasic waveforms mean arterial disease.
Normal flow would not explain his varicose veins and ulcer.
Acute thrombus is a DVT finding; nothing suggests a new DVT.

steps.x: **D. Retrograde flow.** Duplex confirms venous insufficiency.

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman has a 3 month history of a shallow, exudative ulcer above her left medial malleolus with surrounding brown, eczematous skin. There is no surrounding erythema. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 140/80 mmHg. Foot pulses are palpable.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: With ABPI 0.8–1.3 and no infection, four-layer compression bandaging is first-line for an active venous ulcer. Stockings are used only after healing.

steps.x: **Initial** management of an active ulcer.
Active, uninfected venous ulcer; labs show ABPI 0.96 and a normal CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Four-layer compression bandaging**, plus elevation and exercise.

elim: Stockings are not appropriate during active ulceration.
Ablation is definitive treatment of the vein, not the initial step.
No signs of infection and CRP is normal.
Vascular referral is for ABPI >1.3 or significant arterial disease.

steps.x: **C. Four-layer compression bandaging.** ABPI 0.8–1.3: compress.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man's venous ulcer above his right medial malleolus has fully healed after 14 weeks of four-layer compression bandaging. His ABPI is 1.0. He is keen to stop it coming back while he waits for a vascular opinion.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate measure to prevent recurrence?
practice.e: Once healed, Class II compression stockings prevent recurrence. Antibiotics, antiplatelets and anticoagulants do not treat venous hypertension.

steps.x: Long-term prevention after healing.
Healed ulcer with safe ABPI: compression continues as stockings.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Class II compression stockings**.

elim: Antibiotics treat infection; there is none.
Aspirin is for arterial disease, not venous.
Steroid cream treats venous eczema, not ulcer recurrence.
Warfarin treats DVT, not chronic venous hypertension.

steps.x: **A. Class II stockings.** Bandages heal; stockings prevent.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with a venous ulcer above her left medial malleolus has 3 days of spreading redness and warmth around it. She had a widespread rash and lip swelling after amoxicillin. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. She is otherwise well.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
practice.e: An infected venous ulcer is treated with flucloxacillin, but with true penicillin allergy clarithromycin is used. Co-amoxiclav is a penicillin and is for severe infection.

steps.x: Antibiotic choice: check for **allergy** and severity.

clues: rash and lip swelling after amoxicillin
steps.x: Mild-moderate infected ulcer in a true (angioedema) penicillin allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clarithromycin**.

elim: Amoxicillin is the drug that caused the reaction.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin and is reserved for severe infection.
Flucloxacillin is first-line only if not penicillin-allergic.
Phenoxymethylpenicillin is a penicillin.

steps.x: **B. Clarithromycin.** Penicillin-allergic infected ulcer.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has a chronic venous ulcer above her right medial malleolus. The skin around it is stained reddish-brown and feels firm. Her ABPI is 1.0. A biopsy of the pigmented skin shows iron-containing granules in dermal macrophages.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of the skin pigmentation?
practice.e: Venous hypertension forces red cells out of capillaries; their breakdown leaves haemosiderin (iron) in dermal macrophages, giving brown skin.

steps.x: A mechanism question about the brown skin.
Iron in macrophages is haemosiderin; firm skin is lipodermatosclerosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemosiderin** from leaked red cells.

elim: Bilirubin gives yellow jaundice, not iron granules.
Carotene gives orange palms and soles.
Melanocyte proliferation gives naevi or melanoma, not iron.
Methaemoglobin causes cyanosis, not dermal pigment.

steps.x: **C. Haemosiderin.** Leaked red cells break down into iron pigment.

prompts.q: What is a venous ulcer and how does it form?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the pressure problem, then the chain to skin death.

points.p: Chronic skin ulcer from venous hypertension (chronic venous insufficiency)
points.why: It is the most common type of leg ulcer.

points.p: High pressure causes oedema and impairs capillary/lymphatic drainage
points.why: Fluid in the tissue blocks nutrient exchange.

points.p: Skin is starved of oxygen and nutrients and dies
points.why: That is why it is slow to heal.

prompts.q: What are the risk factors for a venous ulcer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: anything that causes venous stasis.

points.p: Varicose veins
Previous DVT
Obesity
Immobility
points.why: Calf muscle pump is not used.

prompts.q: Describe the classic venous ulcer: site, look, pain and surrounding skin.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem will give you these; you must recognise them.

points.p: Gaiter region, classically medial malleolus
points.why: Lateral or toe sites point away from venous.

points.p: Shallow, oozing/exudative, irregular edges
Only mildly painful
Brown skin (haemosiderin, lipodermatosclerosis), venous eczema, oedema
points.why: These skin changes are the giveaway in SBAs.

points.p: Aching legs and night cramps after standing

prompts.q: Which features tell you a leg ulcer is venous rather than arterial?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the distractor is almost always arterial ulcer.

points.p: Venous: medial malleolus; arterial: toes, heel, pressure points
Venous shallow and irregular; arterial punched-out
points.why: Punched-out with pale base is arterial.

points.p: Venous mildly painful; arterial very painful, worse at night
points.why: Arterial rest pain eases with the leg hanging down.

points.p: Venous: pulses present, ABPI >0.8; arterial: weak pulses, low ABPI

prompts.q: What is the signature leg shape, and what are the complications and red flags?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: know when it is no longer 'simple venous'.

points.p: Inverted champagne bottle leg
points.why: Ankle narrowed by lipodermatosclerosis, calf swollen above.

points.p: Chronic non-healing ulcer; progressive lipodermatosclerosis and eczema
Secondary cellulitis
Rapidly worsening pain, necrosis or systemic illness: think arterial or severe infection

prompts.q: What must be done before compression, and which ABPI values matter?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ABPI is the initial investigation in almost every stem.

points.p: Check peripheral pulses, then measure ABPI
ABPI typically normal (>0.8) in venous ulcer
ABPI >1.3 means calcified, non-compressible vessels
points.why: Common in diabetes and CKD: falsely high.

prompts.q: How is the diagnosis confirmed, and what does the confirmatory test show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical diagnosis plus ABPI; duplex confirms the venous cause.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis supported by ABPI
Duplex ultrasound
Shows retrograde venous flow (reflux)

prompts.q: What is the treatment of a venous ulcer, from first-line to definitive?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bandage, then stocking, then ablation.

points.p: Exclude arterial disease with ABPI first
Four-layer compression bandaging (ABPI 0.8–1.3)
Elevation, exercise, weight loss
Healed: Class II compression stockings
Definitive: endovenous ablation (laser or radiofrequency)

prompts.q: How do you manage an infected ulcer, and an ABPI above 1.3?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the two side branches of the pathway.

points.p: Flucloxacillin first-line
Clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic
Co-amoxiclav for severe infection
ABPI >1.3: avoid compression, refer to vascular surgery

prompts.q: Why do venous ulcers form at the medial malleolus, and why is the skin brown?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tie the pressure to the site, and the pigment to red cells.

points.p: Valvular incompetence or outflow obstruction causes sustained venous hypertension
points.why: After DVT or with varicose veins.

points.p: Venous pressure is highest over the medial malleolus
points.why: So capillary perfusion fails there first.

points.p: Haemosiderin from broken-down extravasated red cells

prompts.q: Why does compression work, why can it be dangerous, and why the champagne-bottle shape?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the ABPI rule from first principles.

points.p: Counters venous hypertension, improves venous return and reduces oedema
On a poorly perfused limb it can cause critical ischaemia
Lipodermatosclerosis fibroses the ankle while the calf stays oedematous
points.why: Gives the tapering inverted champagne bottle.

glossary.venous hypertension: Persistently raised pressure in the leg veins, usually from leaky valves or blocked outflow.
glossary.chronic venous insufficiency: Long-term failure of the leg veins to return blood to the heart, causing pooling and high pressure.
glossary.gaiter region: The lower leg between the ankle and mid-calf, where a gaiter would sit.
glossary.medial malleolus: The bony bump on the inner side of the ankle, at the lower end of the tibia.
glossary.lipodermatosclerosis: Hard, brown, fibrosed skin and fat of the lower leg from chronic venous inflammation.
glossary.haemosiderin: Iron-storage pigment left when red cells break down; stains the skin brown.
glossary.venous eczema: Itchy, red, scaly skin of the lower leg caused by venous hypertension.
glossary.inverted champagne bottle: Leg shape in chronic venous disease: narrow fibrosed ankle below a swollen calf.
glossary.ABPI: Ankle-brachial pressure index: ankle systolic divided by arm systolic; normal about 0.9 to 1.3.
glossary.duplex ultrasound: Ultrasound combining images with Doppler flow, showing the direction and speed of blood in vessels.
glossary.retrograde venous flow: Blood flowing back down a vein through incompetent valves; also called reflux.
glossary.reflux: Backward flow of blood through leaky vein valves.
glossary.DVT: Deep vein thrombosis: a clot in a deep vein, which can damage valves and cause venous insufficiency.
glossary.post-thrombotic: Describes leg damage, especially valve failure, that follows a previous DVT.
glossary.varicose veins: Dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by incompetent valves.
glossary.venous stasis: Slow or pooled blood flow in the veins.
glossary.four-layer compression bandage: Graduated multilayer bandage system that applies sustained pressure to heal venous ulcers.
glossary.Class II compression stockings: Medium-pressure stockings worn after healing to stop venous ulcers recurring.
glossary.endovenous ablation: Closing a refluxing vein from inside using laser or radiofrequency heat.
glossary.radiofrequency ablation: Using heat from radio waves through a catheter to seal a vein shut.
glossary.cellulitis: Spreading bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue: red, hot, swollen and tender.
glossary.flucloxacillin: Penicillin antibiotic active against Staphylococcus aureus; first-line for infected ulcers and cellulitis.
glossary.clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic used for skin infection when the patient is penicillin-allergic.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid; a broad penicillin used for severe infection.
glossary.arterial ulcer: Painful, punched-out ulcer on toes or pressure points caused by poor arterial supply.
glossary.neuropathic ulcer: Painless ulcer on pressure areas of the sole, usually in diabetes with loss of sensation.
glossary.pyoderma gangrenosum: Very painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge, linked to IBD and rheumatoid arthritis.
glossary.calcified vessels: Arteries stiffened by calcium, common in diabetes and CKD, giving falsely high ABPI.
glossary.critical ischaemia: Blood supply so poor that the limb is threatened, with rest pain or tissue loss.
glossary.extravasated: Leaked out of a blood vessel into the surrounding tissue.
glossary.calf muscle pump: Calf muscles squeezing deep veins during walking to push blood back to the heart.
glossary.incompetent valves: Vein valves that no longer close properly, letting blood fall back down the leg.
glossary.exudate: Fluid that oozes from an ulcer or inflamed tissue.
